newsitem.title: GERMANY: Speaker breaks ground for Berlin parliament office.
newsitem.headline: Speaker breaks ground for Berlin parliament office.

text.p: Germany's parliamentary speaker Rita Suessmuth broke the ground on Monday for a new office complex for members of parliament near the Reichstag in the country's new capital.
The buildings, due to house around two thirds of the offices and committee rooms of parliamentarians and cost around 900 million marks ($537 million), should be finished by the end of 1999.
The 2,000 room complex will encompass three old buildings and will be called the Dorotheenbloecke, after Dorothea, a 17th century countess who gave her name to the district of Berlin.
The lower house of parliament is due to move into the Reichstag building -- only used occasionally for formal events since the end of World War Two -- by the end of 1999.

Suessmuth, the speaker of the lower house , said the start of the building of the complex was a visible sign of the will of the German parliament to move to Berlin and said the building's design would fit well into the city.

Berlin's mayor Eberhard Diepgen said some space would be reserved in the new complex for a memorial dedicated to people shot trying to escape from the former East Germany across the Berlin Wall, which ran behind the Reichstag.
Diepgen said the new government quarter would reflect Germany's democratic self-confidence.
The costs of developing the new Berlin government and parliament district are expected to hit 1.24 billion marks, above an earlier forecast of 1.13 billion.
Clearing building sites of explosives left over from World War Two has pushed up costs.
Earlier this month Chancellor Helmut Kohl broke the ground for Berlin's new chancellery, a 400-million mark complex, 500 metres (yards) west of the Reichstag.
The groundbreaking for the chancellery marked a symbolic point of no return for the government's move from the former western capital of Bonn.
Parliament voted in 1991 to move to Berlin but planning feuds brought long delays. ($ = 1.676 German Marks)
